summary:
Lunar Crew: Outpost Rescue is a 3D mission trainer for kids that runs in any browser, including phones, with nothing to install. A landing accident strands the player’s crew on the Moon. To survive until rescue, they salvage supplies, repair equipment, share out suit oxygen, power, air and food, grow crops, drive a rover and contact Earth. Every decision has a trade-off, so children practise thinking like an astronaut, not just reading about it.

Real NASA data drives the key moments. The solar-storm drill replays the real May 2024 storm: NASA DONKI flare and solar-particle records trigger the warning, and NASA OSDR RadLab readings from LRO’s CRaTER detector set when the danger rises and falls. Afterwards, players compare their choice with the real readings. The greenhouse and science cards use NASA OSDR studies on space-grown chile peppers, muscle and bone loss, radiation and astronaut immune health. The radio panel shows a real NASA EPIC image of Earth, and CSA youth resources explain what crops need. A “How the data works” page separates real records from simplified game rules.

Kids make the choices astronauts make, using real NASA data.
details:
P/S:Best experienced on a desktop browser (Chrome/Edge); the mobile version is still in progress.

WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Crew: Outpost Rescue is a free 3D browser game that trains kids to think like astronauts. A landing accident strands their crew on the Moon. Over 7 mission days they keep the outpost alive until rescue arrives: restore power, seal an air leak, contact Earth, survive a compressed lunar night, recover landing data and prepare for pickup.

HOW IT WORKS

- Players explore the outpost in third person (keyboard or touch stick). They jump in real Moon gravity, hammer rocks, drive a rover on sample trips and grow food in a greenhouse.

- Four shared resources (suit oxygen, power, base air and food) force real trade-offs. The air maker shares power with other devices, and solar power stops in darkness. Closing a leaking room's door saves air, but the crew loses that room.

- Each player picks a role (Engineer, Scientist or Pilot). Each role has a special move, and each move has a cost.

- PIP, a robot companion, guides each step. A mission journal, outpost radar, daily bonus missions and collectible mission patches keep players exploring.

- If the air runs out, players simply retry the day.

HOW WE USE NASA RESOURCES

Every real number in the game carries a label: LIVE (fetched now), ARCHIVED (real past data), SIMPLIFIED (game rule) or COMPUTED (today's formula).

- NASA DONKI (api.nasa.gov): at mission start, this week's real CMEs and solar particle events set the storm strength (strong, medium or mild). Offline, the game uses the archived 10 May 2024 particle event.

- NASA OSDR RadLab: the solar-storm drill replays 9–12 May 2024 hour by hour from the LRO CRaTER (lunar orbit) and ISS DOSTEL detectors, at 1 game second = 1 real hour. Afterwards, a "Your choice vs the real storm" card adds up the real readings for the hours the player spent outside.

- NASA OSDR studies: OSD-772 (chile peppers grown for 137 days on the ISS) is compared with the player's own harvest. OSD-342 (muscle and bone loss), OSD-360 (radiation) and OSD-903 (astronaut recovery) appear in science cards and the crew health log.

- NASA EPIC: the radio panel shows NASA's newest photo of the whole Earth, taken from the DSCOVR spacecraft. - NASA Moon Fact Sheet: Moon gravity (1.62 m/s²) shapes every jump, and the Earth–Moon distance checks the radio delay the game computes for today.

- CSA food-production toolkit: explains why crops need light, water and nutrients.

- A real ISS air leak (news report and NASA blog) inspired the leak-control mechanic.

BENEFITS

- Kids learn by deciding, not by reading: every choice has a visible consequence.

- It's free and needs no install or account. One link or one file runs on laptops, tablets and phones, even offline.

- A "How the data works" page and parent/teacher notes show adults exactly what is real and what is simplified. INTENDED IMPACT We want children to see NASA open data as something they can use, and to understand why astronauts keep reserves, shelter from space weather and grow food far from Earth. The game is built for classrooms and homes with limited devices or slow internet.

TOOLS

- Languages: JavaScript, HTML and CSS. - three.js r180 (WebGL) for 3D. All models are built in code, with no downloaded 3D assets.

- Web Audio API for synthesized sound, and Canvas/SVG for textures and charts.

- A Node.js build script that packs everything into a single 2 MB HTML file.

- Data scripts that keep the raw NASA downloads with SHA-256 hashes, so every number can be rebuilt.

- Hardware: none beyond an ordinary computer or phone. - AI: parts of the code were written with AI assistance (Claude Code), as disclosed under the Space Apps rules.

WHY IT IS CREATIVE

- The real Sun changes the game: this week's space weather sets how strong your storm drill is.

- Detector data becomes something kids can feel: a "radiation river" rises and falls exactly when the 2024 storm did.

- Kids compare their own decisions with real NASA readings.

- A "Real data" button dims the scene and tags everything that comes from real data, with its source. - From the title screen, anyone can try the real storm in 2 minutes.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Honesty: archived data is never shown as live. Risk bars are teaching values, not medical doses, and the game explains that a shelter does not undo exposure you already received.

- Children: short text, a guiding companion, retries instead of game over, and no purchases.

- Access: touch and keyboard controls, reduced-motion support, screen-reader labels and keyboard-friendly dialogs.

- Privacy and reliability: no accounts, and progress is saved only in the browser. Live requests go only to api.nasa.gov, with a 4-second limit and a 3-hour cache, and fall back to labelled archived data.
